extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of comparative anatomy/physical anthropology
extracted.subtask_description: Detailed anatomical comparison of Man, the great apes (Gorilla, Orang, Chimpanzee), and lower apes/monkeys, focusing on skeleton, skull, dentition, hand/foot, musculature, and brain to assess degrees of similarity and difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertebral column characters (number and curvature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare number of dorsal and lumbar vertebrae and the degree/shape of spinal curves (especially lumbar convexity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and contrasts: Gorillas sometimes have fourteen dorsal pairs; an Orang-Utan skeleton recorded 12 dorsal and 5 lumbar (as in Man). Many lower apes possess 12 dorsal and 6 or 7 lumbar; Douroucouli 14 dorsal and 8 lumbar; a Lemur (Stenops tardigradus) 15 dorsal and 9 lumbar. The vertebral column of the Gorilla differs from Man chiefly in less marked curves, particularly a slighter lumbar convexity; curves are obvious in young Gorilla and Chimpanzee skeletons preserved with ligaments, while young Orangutan columns may be straight or even concave forwards. Use both counts and curvature/shape for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pelvis morphology and relationship to posture
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess pelvis shape and proportions (haunch bones, pelvic passage, ischiatic prominences) as indicators of support for erect posture and muscle attachments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human pelvis: expanded haunch bones afford visceral support in erect posture and provide space for muscles that maintain upright attitude. Gorilla pelvis differs considerably (see Fig. 15). Gibbon pelvis is more different from Gorilla than Gorilla is from Man — e.g., flat narrow haunch bones, long narrow passage, coarse outwardly curved ischiatic prominences with 'callosities' present in some apes but absent in Gorilla, Chimpanzee, Orang, and Man. Lower monkeys and Lemurs show progressively more quadrupedal pelvis characteristics. Use pelvic proportions and presence/absence of features (callosities, shape of haunch bones) to evaluate functional and classificatory differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skull proportions: face vs braincase, occipital foramen, brow ridges
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare relative predominance of facial bones versus cranial cavity, position of occipital foramen, and development of supraciliary (brow) crests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Gorilla the face (massive jaw-bones) predominates over the brain case; in Man the proportions are reversed. Occipital foramen in Man is placed just behind the centre of the skull base (balanced for erect posture); in Gorilla it lies in the posterior third. Human skull surface is comparatively smooth with little brow projection; Gorilla shows vast crests and overhanging brow ridges. Note that some apparent 'defects' (e.g., flattened forehead) may result from facial bone overdevelopment rather than deficient cranial vault; sections can reveal true cranial curve. Use these proportional characters, and beware of superficial appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cranial capacity and its comparative interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use absolute and relative cranial cavity volumes, and their ranges within groups, to assess differences between humans and apes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported measures: no adult human cranium observed with less than 62 cubic inches (Morton's smallest 63); most capacious gorilla measured ~34.5 cubic inches. Humans show a wider absolute range (smallest to largest ~62 to 114 cubic inches) than the difference between highest ape and lowest human; gorilla crania among themselves differ nearly one-third (34.5 to 24 cubic inches). Therefore consider both absolute volumes and within-group variability — differences within Homo can exceed differences between Homo and highest apes; relative proportions are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dentition as classificatory criterion (number, form, succession, diastema, canines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate number and kinds of teeth (milk and permanent), crown morphology, presence of diastema, canine size/shape, root complexity, molar cusp patterns, and order of eruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human milk teeth: 4 incisors, 2 canines, 4 molars per jaw (20 total). Human permanent: 4 incisors, 2 canines, 4 premolars, 6 molars per jaw (32 total). Gorilla similar in number and general crown pattern but differs in diastema (break in series to accommodate opposing canines), very large projecting canines, more complex roots of false molars, different relative molar sizes, more complex crown of hindmost lower grinder, and different eruption order (permanent canines appear before 2nd and 3rd molars in Man, after them in Gorilla). Other primates vary: Cebus (New World) milk 24, permanent 36; Marmosets have same total as humans but different composition (more false molars, fewer true molars); Lemurs show pronounced differences, some approaching rodent-like dentition (Aye-Aye). Teeth are asserted to have 'peculiar classificatory value' and are often more trustworthy indicators of affinity than other characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand vs foot terminal-division criteria (distinguishing hand from foot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether a terminal limb division is a hand or a foot by key anatomical characters rather than superficial mobility or proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit absolute anatomical differences (listed as distinguishing the human foot from the hand): 1) arrangement of the tarsal bones; 2) presence of a short flexor and a short extensor muscle of the digits; 3) possession of the muscle termed 'peronaeus longus'. Use these characters (bone arrangement and muscle complement) as the definitive test. Superficial opposability or toe mobility may vary without changing the organ's fundamental identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musculotendinous arrangement of hand and foot (long vs short flexors, tendon interrelations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare which flexor/extensor muscles are 'long' (muscle belly in limb, tendons into digits) vs 'short' (belly in palm/sole), the distinctness or commingling of tendons, and accessory fleshy bundles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the human hand, principal flexors and extensors are long muscles with distinct tendons remaining separate through the palm. In the foot there are also three principal flexors and extensors but one extensor and one flexor are short (fleshy parts in back/sole). Tendons of the long flexor of the toes and of the great toe become united and commingled in the sole and receive an accessory muscle connected with the heel bone; in Gorillas the tendons interlace slightly differently and an accessory fleshy bundle exists. Lower apes exaggerate these deviations (multiple slips attaching to long flexor tendons or multiplication of slips). Use the pattern of muscle origin/location, tendon distinctness/interlacing, and accessory slips to compare taxa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brain structural criteria (corpus callosum, posterior lobe, posterior cornu, hippocampus minor, convolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess brain differences by presence/absence and development of the corpus callosum, posterior lobe and its posterior cornu, the hippocampus minor/major, and degree of cortical convolution (sulci and gyri), and the relative development of cerebral hemispheres vs cerebellum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major organizational shift: appearance of the 'corpus callosum' in placental mammals is described as a great and sudden modification. Increased cerebral complexity is primarily the disproportionate development of cerebral hemispheres (especially posterior lobe) relative to other parts, leading to overlap/hiding of the cerebellum from above. The posterior cornu and the hippocampus minor are associated with a well-developed posterior lobe; their presence/size are diagnostic. Degree of surface convolution (number of sulci and convolutions) increases toward higher mammals (Elephant, Porpoise, higher Apes, Man). Comparative examples: all Marmoset/American monkeys/old-world monkeys/baboons/man-like apes have cerebellum hidden posteriorly and possess large posterior cornu/hippocampus minor, whereas every Lemur examined retains cerebellum partially visible from above with rudimentary posterior lobe. The author emphasizes the continuity of gradations from lower brains to near-man levels and points out that the one true structural break lies between lemurs and other simians rather than between man and apes.
